extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write mathematical proofs / introductory proofs course
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for composing correct and clear mathematical proofs, including techniques (direct, cases, contrapositive, contradiction) and principles of mathematical writing for undergraduate proof-writing tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove conditional statements by assuming the hypothesis P and deducing the conclusion Q. Work forward from assumptions to reach the desired conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the assumption 'Suppose P' and use definitions and algebraic/logical manipulation to derive Q. It can be helpful to map a strategy by working backwards to something obviously true and then reversing the steps. Use previously proved results when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When an expression or statement behaves differently under distinct mutually exclusive scenarios (e.g., n even vs odd), split the proof into cases and prove the statement in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the relevant partition of possibilities and treat each separately. Examples: prove an expression is a multiple of 4 by handling n even and n odd. After covering all cases, conclude the statement holds generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating similar cases / 'Without loss of generality' (WLOG)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more cases are nearly identical except for a symmetric difference (e.g., m even & n odd vs m odd & n even), it is acceptable to do one case in detail and indicate the other is similar using 'Without loss of generality...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises avoiding the abbreviation 'WLOG' for transparency and recommends, at least until experienced, writing out all cases even if similar. If using WLOG, clearly state the symmetry that justifies omitting the other case(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backwards as a proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Map out a strategy by working backwards from the desired conclusion to something obviously true; then reverse the steps in the formal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove 2√(xy) ≤ x + y, square both sides to reach 0 ≤ (x−y)^2, which is obviously true; then reverse the steps, noting when operations (like squaring) preserve inequality conditions. Ensure intermediate steps are reversible and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution when taking square roots or applying monotone operations
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying operations such as taking square roots or multiplying/dividing by quantities, ensure the operation does not change inequality direction or require additional hypotheses (e.g., nonnegativity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the example, after obtaining 4xy ≤ (x+y)^2 one may take square roots without reversing the ≤ sign because both sides are nonnegative; this follows from a previous proposition. Always cite the relevant theorem that justifies such a step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use previously proved propositions/theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs may and should rely on earlier propositions/theorems; cite them when a step depends on previously established results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that often a proof uses another proved proposition, and you should reference it (e.g., 'by the previous proposition' when taking square roots of nonnegative sides). Proper use of prior results strengthens and shortens proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive proof (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P then Q', prove the contrapositive 'If not Q then not P'. Begin by assuming ¬Q and deduce ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard outline: 'Suppose ¬Q. ... Therefore ¬P.' Use this method when it is easier to transform information about the conclusion into information about the hypothesis. Include any intermediate logical/arithmetical steps and cite DeMorgan's laws when negating compound statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DeMorgan's laws and negation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs use negated statements (e.g., in contrapositive or contradiction), apply correct logical negation rules (DeMorgan's laws, negation of quantifiers) to transform and reason about the statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: negating '5 | x and 5 | y' gives '5 ∤ x or 5 ∤ y' and should be handled with separate cases. For universal statements, remember ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), which often yields a specific counterexample in contradiction proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a statement P, assume ¬P and deduce a contradiction (some statement C and its negation ¬C). Conclude P must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard outline: 'Suppose ¬P. ... Therefore C ∧ ¬C.' The contradiction may be any clearly false statement (e.g., 1 is even) and need not be tautological. Use this method especially when direct approaches lack a clear starting assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving conditional statements by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P then Q' via contradiction, assume P and ¬Q (equivalently assume ¬(P ⇒ Q)) and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: 'Suppose P and ¬Q. ... Therefore C ∧ ¬C.' This yields a direct contradiction arising under the assumption that P holds while Q fails; conclude P ⇒ Q. The text demonstrates this on algebraic parity examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine proof techniques as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex proofs may combine direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction, and case analysis within a single argument; use whichever technique is most appropriate for subclaims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: begin with a direct approach, but inside the proof, establish an auxiliary claim by contradiction. Be explicit about the nested proof structure and which technique is used at each stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin sentences with a word, not a mathematical symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Start each sentence with a word (or words) rather than a mathematical symbol to avoid ambiguity and capitalization issues (symbols are case-sensitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'A is a subset of B.' Good: 'The set A is a subset of B.' Bad: 'x is an integer, so 2x+5 is an integer.' Good: 'Because x is an integer, 2x+5 is an integer.' Follow conventional sentence capitalization and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: End sentences with a period, even when ending with math
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mathematical statements at sentence ends like English phrases: always punctuation (periods) should terminate sentences, even if the final token is a symbol or formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a period after displayed or inline formulas when they conclude sentences. This keeps punctuation consistent and text grammatically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate mathematical symbols and expressions with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words to separate mathematical expressions so distinct expressions don't run together and cause ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Because x^2 − 1 = 0, x = 1 or x = −1.' Better: 'Because x^2 − 1 = 0, it follows that x = 1 or x = −1.' Insert connective words to enhance clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse of symbols (symbols are not words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use mathematical symbols as replacements for words in prose; symbols are appropriate inside formulas but are out of place in ordinary sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Since the two sets are =, one is a subset of the other.' Good: 'Since the two sets are equal, one is a subset of the other.' Similarly, avoid writing logical implications like 'x odd ⇒ x^2 odd' in running text without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using unnecessary symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce symbols or notation that obscure rather than clarify; prefer plain English when it is clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'No set X has negative cardinality.' Better: 'No set has negative cardinality.' Avoid gratuitous formal notation that adds cognitive load without benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first person plural ('we')
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematical writing it is common to address the reader with 'we' rather than 'I' or 'you,' guiding the reader through the argument collaboratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' to present steps and lead the reader. This style is conventional and pedagogically friendly in proofs and expository text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions over passive ones to make writing more lively and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad (passive): 'The value x = 3 is obtained through division of both sides by 5.' Good (active): 'Dividing both sides by 5, we get x = 3.' Active voice improves readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain each new symbol when introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a new symbol is introduced in a proof, explicitly explain its meaning so readers are not forced to search backwards for its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Since a | b, it follows that b = ac.' Good: 'Since a | b, it follows that b = ac for some integer c.' Always state the domain/type of newly introduced variables (e.g., integer c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous pronouns like 'it'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use pronouns when their referent is unclear; replace with explicit nouns to avoid reader confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Since X ⊆ Y, and 0 < |X|, we see that it is not empty.' (Which is 'it'?) Good: 'Since X ⊆ Y and 0 < |X|, we see that Y is not empty.' Make pronoun antecedents explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of inference words (since, because, as, for, so)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'since' and 'because' assert that the preceding clause is true and that the subsequent clause follows; ensure both the asserted premise and the inference are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructions assert P and then Q because of P; they are not merely conditional. Use them only when you mean to claim P is true and that Q follows. Be precise to avoid inadvertent logical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adverbs of logical consequence ('thus', 'hence', 'therefore') correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Place these words before statements that logically follow from previous sentences; ensure the following statement actually follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use such adverbs to introduce statements that are not consequences of prior text. Check that the logical inference is valid before writing 'Therefore ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity is the gold standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize clarity above rigid adherence to stylistic rules; if breaking a rule improves clarity, do so judiciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your mathematical writing should evolve with practice. Read and emulate good proofs; adopt what works and avoid what doesn't. The main criterion for choices of notation, structure, and style is whether they make the argument clearer to the reader.
